section_summary: This section assembles U.S. diplomatic and military records from 1940–1944 concerning Japanese propaganda, espionage, recruitment, and sabotage activities in China. It includes translations of Japanese air-dropped leaflets, a Chinese official’s anti-Western essay, detailed intelligence on suspected agents in Qingdao, reports of Nanjing recruitment efforts and arrests, and warnings about General Kenji Doihara’s alleged operations in South China. Later documents describe propaganda surrounding Hong Kong and the Pacific War and investigate the suspected collaboration of broadcaster George Chow.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese handbill and anti-foreign article
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to despatch no. 209 concerning a Japanese handbill and a translated anti-foreign article.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Ward at Foochow's handbill and anti-foreign article, original in file 711.90/63.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 209: Transmitting Japanese handbill and anti-foreign article
subfiles.from: Robert S. Ward, American Consul, Foochow
subfiles.about: Transmits a copy of despatch no. 177 and its Japanese propaganda and Chinese newspaper enclosures.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 209: Ward forwards a Japanese handbill scattered over southern Fujian with translation, and Hou Hsuen-yu's article 'The Morals of Present Day Diplomats'.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 177: Japanese handbill and “The Morals of Present Day Diplomats”
subfiles.from: Robert S. Ward, American Consul, Foochow
subfiles.about: Analyzes a Japanese propaganda handbill and an anti-Western article by a senior Fujian official.
subfiles.summary: Ward describes a Japanese leaflet that represented Stephen Early’s comments on the Monroe Doctrine as proof that the United States would leave Asia to Japan. He then summarizes Hoü Hsüen-yü’s attack on American trade with Japan, British diplomacy, and Western violations of the five Confucian virtues. Ward argues that both documents exploit the collapse of French and British prestige and Chinese uncertainty about American policy, warning that an apparent American abandonment of China could encourage accommodation with Japan.

subfiles.title: Original Japanese propaganda handbill
subfiles.about: Presents the Chinese-language original of a Japanese handbill on a supposed world-wide Monroe Doctrine.
subfiles.summary: Japanese handbill uses reports of Roosevelt and Early's statements to claim Germany, Japan and the US should control Europe, Asia and the Americas, mocking Chinese reliance on Western aid.

subfiles.title: Translation of a propaganda pamphlet dropped over southern Fukien
subfiles.from: Japanese propagandists; translated by the American Consulate
subfiles.about: Translates a leaflet claiming that American non-intervention leaves Asian affairs to Japanese leadership.
subfiles.summary: The leaflet quotes reports about Roosevelt and Stephen Early to argue that the United States will neither enter the European war nor interfere in East Asia. It says Germany and Italy will manage Europe and Japan will lead Asia, while Britain and France collapse. A boxed article ridicules Chinese dependence on foreign help and calls American non-intervention its only sincere policy.

subfiles.title: “The Morals of Present Day Diplomats”
subfiles.to: Readers of the Nan Fang Jih Pao and U.S. diplomatic officials
subfiles.about: Condemns Western and Japanese diplomacy as violations of the five traditional Chinese virtues.
subfiles.summary: Hoü contrasts benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and truthfulness with what he portrays as the utilitarian deceit of modern diplomacy. He attacks American material support for Japan, British closure of the Burma Road, Allied conduct toward France, Axis treatment of Chinese representatives, and repeated Western breaches of promises. Although also condemning Japan for copying Western methods, he asserts that China’s adherence to its traditional virtues will ultimately prevail.

subfiles.title: War Department letter of transmittal to A. A. Berle Jr.
subfiles.from: Sherman Miles, Military Intelligence Division, G-2
subfiles.to: A. A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards intelligence summaries on suspected Qingdao espionage agents and Fritz Heberling.
subfiles.summary: Miles sends Berle two MID communications: suspected espionage agents in Qingdao, and Fritz Heberling of Chicago.

subfiles.title: Summary of information: Suspected espionage agents in Tsingtao, China
subfiles.to: Department of State and intelligence distribution
subfiles.about: Lists Japanese military and naval intelligence organizations, operatives, informants, and cooperating businesses in Qingdao.
subfiles.summary: A source described as reliable supplies an extensive list of alleged Japanese espionage personnel and methods in Qingdao. The report covers the Military Gendarmerie, Seki Detachment, naval intelligence, recruitment in cafés and clubs frequented by American sailors, and alleged penetration of foreign firms and consular staffs. It also profiles Russian, German, Latvian, Chinese, Japanese, and other individuals suspected of furnishing intelligence or acting as intermediaries.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 18: Japanese propaganda in relation to the United States
subfiles.from: C. E. Gauss, American Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese leaflet dropped over Chengdu claiming that strikes and isolationism prevent American aid to China.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 18: a leaflet used a misleading factory photograph and Lindbergh and Hoover speeches to argue labor disputes limit arms production and non-interventionism blocks aid; Gauss thought it unlikely to persuade.

subfiles.title: Departmental digest of Chungking despatch no. 137
subfiles.about: Summarizes Belechenko’s allegations about Nanjing agents recruiting underpaid Chinese officials.
subfiles.summary: The digest states that low salaries, favoritism, graft, inefficiency, and weak discipline made some civilian and military officials vulnerable to recruitment by agents of the Nanjing regime. Such agents allegedly offered transportation and better-paid positions. The Embassy emphasized that it could neither verify nor investigate Belechenko’s claims.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 137: Subversive activities of Nanking agents in unoccupied China
subfiles.from: C. E. Gauss, American Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.about: Transmits a conversation memorandum concerning alleged Nanjing recruitment in unoccupied China.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 137: Gauss forwards Macdonald's memorandum of a talk with Belechenko of the Zunyi Staff College, cautioning the Embassy cannot verify the statements.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation: Subversive activities of Nanking agents
subfiles.about: Records Belechenko’s account of corruption, low pay, poor discipline, and collaborationist recruitment at the Zunyi Staff College.
subfiles.summary: Belechenko alleges Nanjing agents exploit Chungking officials' financial distress with travel expenses and better pay; he cites delayed salaries, misused payroll deposits, favoritism and indiscipline as threats to the Central Government.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Exposure of the Chung Ioh Company in Singapore
subfiles.about: References a report alleging that a Hong Kong company served as a Japanese agent in a South Pacific fifth-column organization.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 1316: Hong Kong's Chung Ioh Company allegedly a Japanese-Wang Ching-wei agent in Singapore tied to a South Pacific fifth column.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 392: Japanese propaganda leaflets dropped in Fukien
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.about: Transmits Edward E. Rice’s report and translations of Japanese leaflets dropped in unoccupied Fujian.
subfiles.summary: Vincent forwards a despatch from Consul Rice, formerly at Fuzhou and then traveling to Chongqing. The enclosed originals and translations describe Japanese military victories and urge Chinese cooperation in building a Greater East Asia “New Order.”

subfiles.title: Rice report on leaflets dropped at Changchow
subfiles.from: Edward E. Rice, American Consul, in transit at Nanping
subfiles.to: Clarence E. Gauss, American Ambassador, Chungking
subfiles.about: Forwards Japanese leaflets dropped at Zhangzhou on March 20, 1942, with suggested translations.
subfiles.summary: Rice encloses leaflets dropped by Japanese aircraft at Changchow claiming heavy Allied losses and urging Chinese to join Japan against the US and Britain for a new Asian order.

subfiles.title: Chinese original: Manifesto to the peoples of Greater East Asia
subfiles.about: Urges Asian peoples to cooperate with Japan and overthrow Britain and the United States.
subfiles.summary: The Chinese-language leaflet presents Japan’s war as an anti-colonial campaign to emancipate Asia and establish a co-prosperity order. It invokes Tojo, condemns Chinese reliance on Britain and America, celebrates Japanese conquests, and includes a map or graphic of the expanding war. Its reverse supplies purported statistics of Allied losses.

subfiles.title: Suggested translation: “Manifesto to Brothers of the Great East Asiatic Races”
subfiles.from: Japanese military propagandists; translated by Edward E. Rice’s office
subfiles.to: Asian public and American diplomatic readers
subfiles.about: Translates a Japanese manifesto portraying the Pacific War as the liberation of Asia.
subfiles.summary: Manifesto to East Asian peoples claims Britain and America provoked the China-Japan conflict, celebrates the fall of Hong Kong, Manila and Singapore, predicts Burma, Java and Australia, and lists Allied losses December 1941-March 1942.

subfiles.title: Translation of a second Japanese leaflet’s loss statistics
subfiles.from: Japanese headquarters; translated by Edward E. Rice’s office
subfiles.to: Chinese public and American diplomatic readers
subfiles.about: Lists exaggerated Japanese claims of Allied warship, cargo-vessel, and aircraft losses.
subfiles.summary: The fragment classifies American, British, and Dutch battleships, carriers, cruisers, and smaller vessels allegedly sunk or damaged. It concludes with totals for cargo tonnage and aircraft destroyed. The document is presented as a translation of the second type of leaflet dropped at Zhangzhou.

subfiles.title: Department of State distribution memorandum for despatch no. 392
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation; Coordinator of Information
subfiles.about: Distributes the Chungking report on Japanese propaganda leaflets to U.S. intelligence agencies.
subfiles.summary: Department circulates confidential Despatch No. 392 with the Fujian propaganda material to military, naval, federal and information authorities.

subfiles.title: Grew despatch: Japanese aviators over Hong Kong
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, aboard the exchange ship S.S. Gripsholm
subfiles.about: Transmits two leaflets dropped by Japanese aviators over Hong Kong before its fall.
subfiles.summary: Grew encloses two Japanese leaflets for Chinese residents and British nationals in Hong Kong, circulated to State and military intelligence.

subfiles.title: Leaflet to Chinese emigrants in Hong Kong
subfiles.about: Calls on Chinese residents to pressure the British to surrender and promises Japanese protection of life and property.
subfiles.summary: Leaflet to Chinese in Hong Kong: Japan seeks to destroy British influence, not Hong Kong; resistance brings looting, cooperation preserves property.

subfiles.title: Leaflet to British nationals in Hong Kong
subfiles.to: British nationals in Hong Kong and Kowloon
subfiles.about: Demands surrender and threatens annihilation if British forces destroy facilities or continue resisting.
subfiles.summary: Leaflet to British nationals claims sweeping Axis victories, including Moscow, and urges civilians to force Hong Kong's surrender, threatening annihilation if installations are destroyed.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding Grew’s Hong Kong propaganda despatch
subfiles.from: John N. Begg, Division of Cultural Relations
subfiles.to: Edward Stanley, Office of War Information
subfiles.about: Sends the Office of War Information a copy of Grew’s despatch and Hong Kong leaflets.
subfiles.summary: Begg forwards Grew's August 8 despatch from the Gripsholm with Japanese leaflets dropped over Hong Kong.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese propaganda in Peiping
subfiles.about: References a report on the rapid expansion of Japanese propaganda in Beijing after December 8, 1941.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 233: Japanese propaganda in Beijing, sporadic before the Pacific War, grew rapidly after December 8.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Alleged British anti-American propaganda in China
subfiles.about: References a communication alleged to show British anti-American propaganda and bearing a Japanese-occupied Beijing date stamp.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 546: alleged British anti-American propaganda in China, bearing a Japanese-occupied Beijing stamp.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Messages radioed from Shanghai to Tokyo
subfiles.about: References copies of radio messages sent from Shanghai to Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Filing sheet on messages radioed between Shanghai and Tokyo; the original letter is filed separately.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 5: Arrest of a Nanking spy
subfiles.from: Harry E. Stevens, Office of the Secretary on Detail at Chengtu
subfiles.about: Reports the arrest of Sichuan official Ch’en Chu-jen as the alleged leader of a Nanjing espionage ring.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 5: Ch'en Chu-jen, a former Sichuan provincial official, was arrested as a Nanjing spy after being lured to a recital, and sent to Chongqing for military trial.

subfiles.title: Department of State transmittal of the Ch’en Chu-jen report
subfiles.about: Forwards despatch no. 5 on the arrest of an alleged Nanjing spy to the OSS.
subfiles.summary: State sends OSS Stevens's confidential February 25 report 'Arrest of a Nanking Spy'.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 2249: Reported arrival of General Kenji Doihara in the Canton area
subfiles.from: C. E. Gauss, American Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.about: Transmits a Guilin airgram alleging that Doihara was directing espionage and sabotage in South China.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 2249: British intelligence places Doihara's headquarters near Guangzhou, with US installations near Guilin as targets; sabotage and paratroop attacks anticipated; Gauss forwards the airgram.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-6: Doihara’s alleged espionage and sabotage operations
subfiles.about: Reports intelligence that Doihara had established a headquarters near Guangzhou and might target Guilin’s aviation facilities.
subfiles.summary: Airgram A-6: British reports and US officers expect Japanese agents to attack Guilin installations; Japanese reprisals against villages that aided American airmen and the beating deaths of two pilots.

subfiles.title: File charge-out record for 894.20293
subfiles.about: Provides blank fields for recording the temporary charge and movement of file 894.20293.
subfiles.summary: File charge-out form for 894.20293; no substantive content.

subfiles.title: War Department summary of information: George Chow
subfiles.about: Profiles George Chow, a Canadian Chinese broadcaster suspected of serving Japanese and Axis interests.
subfiles.summary: George Chow, ex-National City Bank investigator in Hong Kong, a prisoner who claimed escape, then worked at the Japanese-controlled Hong Kong station, raising suspicion; later reported at the British Embassy in Chongqing and traveling toward Canada.
